newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: New Afghan rulers appeal for international aid.
newsitem.headline: New Afghan rulers appeal for international aid.

text.p: Afghanistan's new purist Islamic rulers appealed on Sunday for international aid to help rebuild the war-torn country and said they intended to call a national convention to decide how to form a strong central government.
Acting Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammed Ghous told a news conference that 17 years of war had left Afghanistan facing a disaster with many people unable to feed their families.
"We are hoping that all countries will take part in the reconstruction of our country. The whole administrative system and public services in Afghanistan are paralysed," he said.
"If we don't have cooperation and assistance from foreign countries, it will be very difficult for Afghanistan to stand on its own feet."

Western aid groups already working in Afghanistan -- helping some 200,000 people a day in Kabul alone -- say most of their projects have ground to a halt because they depend on women who are not being allowed to work by the hardline Taleban movement which captured the Afghan capital on September 27.

They intend to appeal to the Taleban, probably on Monday, to find a quick solution to a problem several group leaders say could lead to a shutdown of projects and a halt to the flow of funds from western governments, but Ghous called the issue a "small problem".

"I would like to ask these organisations to continue their cooperation and I am hopeful that these small questions will be resolved in the future," said the 35-year-old Moslem priest from Kandahar, where the Taleban movement is based.

He added that the related issue of women's education, suspended in the three-quarters of Afghanistan the Taleban have captured since their movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago, would have to wait.
"When full security prevails in Afghanistan, this issue will be reconsidered and girls will be allowed to go to school," he said.

He gave no indication of how long that would take. On Saturday, Black-turbanned Taleban fighters started an assault on the Panjshir valley, stronghold of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
Ghous said the Taleban were willing to talk peace with Masood, who defended the valley in the 1980s against repeated assault by Soviet forces backing the then communist government.
"If he is not ready to negotiate, we will continue our campaign in the Panjshir valley," he added.

The valley, entered through a narrow, winding gorge with almost sheer sides, is well defended and few foreign analysts believe the Taleban can take it before the harsh Afghan winter sets in late next month.
Reuter correspondent Jeremy Wagstaff reported from the scene that fighting was less intense than on Saturday, when the Taleban took the heights at the entrance to the gorge.
He said they bombarded Masood outposts after consolidating their hold on the newly captured peaks.

Ghous said the Taleban were also willing to negotiate with a second potential foe, former communist general Abdul Rashid Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek who controls six northern provinces from the city of Mazar-i-Sharif.

Dostum moved tanks and other heavy military equipment south after the Taleban took Kabul and his men say he is prepared to fight if the largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban tried to move north. Ghous said the Taleban would fight if Dostum moved south.
"But we prefer to negotiate with all forces in the conflict because this is in the national interest," he said.
He also said the nations of former Soviet Central Asia had nothing to fear from the Taleban.

"The position of the Taleban Islamic Movement is to restore peace and security within the borders of Afghanistan and establish a strong central government," he said. "It does not intend to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries.
Ghous gave no time frame for a government to replace the Taleban administration, which he called a caretaker governmnnt.

"When true representatives gather, they will form a policy on elections. It will depend on them on whether they want a general election or they want to form a kind of grand assembly to determine the future of the government," he said.
